chapters.title: The Boss Who Checks the Chairs

blocks.text: In ==1970== the French army wrote a report on a young trainee officer from the École Polytechnique. It said he was “inapte à se voir confier un poste de responsabilités”: unfit to be given a post of responsibility. It also said he lacked the authority to impose himself and took little part in teamwork. The trainee was Bernard Arnault, and the file only came out in June 2026, in a critical biography by the historian Audrey Millet.

Half a century later, that same man runs more than 200,000 people and 75 brands. __So how does somebody the army called unfit to lead actually lead?__ Not by giving speeches. He does it mostly by looking at things very closely, and then asking awkward questions about what he saw.
Keep this report in mind the next time someone writes you off.
Saturday morning

Every Saturday morning, Arnault goes shopping, except that he is not buying anything. He walks through stores with a changing group of deputies, bodyguards and his own children. The usual route includes the Dior flagship on Avenue Montaigne, Louis Vuitton inside Galeries Lafayette and the Le Bon Marché department store.

After each tour, his executives get texts and emails listing what is wrong, in what Bloomberg called “bullet points of obsessive detail”. Fortune reported that he has visited as many as ==25 stores in a day==, rivals included. Now 77, he still does it. “And you don't feel that from behind an Excel spreadsheet at a desk,” he told WWD in October 2026, speaking of how a product is really treated on the shop floor.

For example: after one visit to Dubai, his son Alexandre says, the comments ran from the chairs in the store to the shoes the salespeople were wearing. His son Antoine remembers a note from his father about a counter in a Tokyo store. It told him to use a bar Antoine had designed for a Berluti shop about 12 years before. His father still remembered it.
Things that you won't typically notice, but once you've seen tens of thousands of stores over the years, I think it's what comes to your mind immediately.

The habit is older than LVMH. From the age of five or six, Arnault rode with his grandfather to building sites, in a car with a driver, because the old man had no licence. He watched him talk to foremen and workers. By ten, he says, he was annoying his father by pointing at a rival's site and asking how that firm had won the job.

He jokes about it now. “Some store managers joke that I should be hired as director of visual merchandising, after the changes I have regularly suggested in our stores,” he told WWD. In the Legend podcast he added the punchline: he changes a display, comes back a week later, and the manager tells him it is selling better. He admits that this pleases him.
Your best market research is free. Go and stand in the shop.
The shape of his day

Forbes described a day that starts at 6:30 a.m. at home, with classical music, industry news and texts to his family and brand chiefs. Bloomberg gives office hours of 8 a.m. to 8:30 p.m. A 2026 franceinfo profile says he is at his desk on Avenue Montaigne by 8:30, drinks only water and never goes to bed after 11 p.m. Sources differ by half an hour. Nobody disputes the discipline.

Two things break up the work. He keeps a Yamaha grand piano at the office and takes 20-minute breaks to play. And he plays tennis four hours a week, “avec une certaine intensité”, with a certain intensity. His wife, the concert pianist Hélène Mercier-Arnault, is blunt about the rest: “Il n'est pas doué pour les loisirs”, meaning he has no gift for leisure. When he can, though, he goes home to have lunch with her.

blocks.text: He works 24 hours. When he sleeps, he's dreaming of new ideas.
blocks.who: Delphine Arnault, his eldest child, to Forbes, 2019

blocks.text: He also says he tries to protect empty time. He blocks out periods with very few appointments and uses them to meet people from outside business, to hear different ideas on economics or history. “Il faut des moments de réflexion,” he said in 2026: you need moments to think. He admits it does not always work.
What a meeting with him is like

Bloomberg's 2024 profile is the clearest account we have. Meetings start exactly on time. Deputies say they must arrive fully prepared. He sends so many emails, all day and every day, that staff swap tips on how to sort them. The magazine found current staff, former staff and outsiders alike both in awe of him and afraid of him.

The most useful detail is this one. __He hates complacency so much that the worst way to open a meeting with him is to say that sales are robust.__ Good news does not interest him for long, because he is already looking for the next thing to fix. Arnault describes the same habit from his side: “Bon, tout ça, c'est bien, mais ça pourrait être mieux.” All this is fine, but it could be better.
Never walk in with “sales are robust”. Walk in with the problem.

Then there is the lunch. According to people close to him, quoted by the Wall Street Journal in 2023, he gathers his five children once a month in a private dining room at LVMH headquarters. The meal lasts exactly 90 minutes. He reads discussion topics from his iPad, then goes around the table asking each child for advice, including on specific managers and on whether a brand needs a shake-up.

That lunch tells you how he makes decisions. He collects opinions in a set format, from people who have to defend them in front of each other, and then he decides alone. “En dernier ressort, c'est vous qui décidez,” he said of the loneliness of the top job: in the last resort, it is you who decides. He also says he likes being contradicted, “même si quelquefois, je pense qu'ils ont tort”, even when he thinks they are wrong.
Ninety minutes. An iPad. Five children. Imagine preparing for that lunch.
How he hires

Sidney Toledano's story shows the style. Arnault hired him to Dior at the end of 1993 and he signed on 17 January 1994 as director of leather goods. On his first day, at 9 a.m., his phone rang. It was the boss, asking one question: “Have you thought about the bag?” Three months later Toledano showed him a design that became the Lady Dior. He went on to run Dior for nearly 20 years.

For creative people, he looks for something he says you cannot test for. He told Harvard Business Review that the manager's job is choosing artists who secretly want to see their work on the street, even if they would hate to say so. “It's just buried in their DNA,” he said, and learning to see it “just takes experience”. Then you leave them alone. When he wanted a designer to see what Japanese teenagers wore at night, he did not tell him what to copy. He simply said: “Go look.”

His group also takes bets that others find odd. When Louis Vuitton's chief picked Pharrell Williams, a music producer, as men's creative director, many had expected a young fashion-school graduate. Pharrell, who presented his first concept to Arnault and the brand's CEO, described what came next: there were no directives. “They just gave me the keys.”

Loyalty is the other half. Michael Burke joined him as an intern from the EDHEC business school, because he spoke English, and went with him to America in 1981. More than 40 years later Arnault calls him brilliant and says he is still with him, as head of LVMH in the US. “La fidélité, ça compte dans les affaires,” he said: loyalty counts in business. And one thing he says he never forgives: “le mensonge”, the lie.
He started as an intern. Forty-five years later, he's still there.
How much he really delegates

LVMH runs on a split that sounds like a contradiction. Brands keep their own image, products and managers, and Arnault says he tries to run the group “like a start-up” without the reporting that slows people down. Pierre-Yves Roussel, who ran the fashion group, described weekly meetings one floor up in Arnault's office, covering “every single important decision”. In the same breath he said: “The group works by delegation, too.”

So you get real freedom inside a very tight watch. Toledano puts the upside simply: “Decisions are made quickly.” He contrasts that with bosses appointed by investment funds, and calls his 30 years with Arnault the best part of his working life. Not everyone would describe it that way, and that side of the story deserves equal space.
Quick decisions are a start-up's edge. He kept his at 200,000 people.
The other side of the desk

Critics describe a climate of fear. The INA's media review says the group's headquarters is often compared to the Sun King's court, and quotes journalists who say staff want to meet far from work and refuse to be recorded. In December 2025 France 2's Cash Investigation interviewed former LVMH managers who described how the group is run, and Mediapart summed up the programme's picture as including brutal management. LVMH refused contact for more than nine months, the programme's reporter says, and defenders of the group called the show one-sided.

Then there is the memo. In January 2024 he told staff not to speak to a named list of media outlets, warning that a breach “will be considered a serious infraction, with the corresponding consequences attached to it”, according to the Financial Times, as reported by Fortune. Journalists from across French media, including his own papers, signed a letter calling the ban illegal.

Against that, WWD notes that LVMH ranks very highly among Europe's most desired employers, and Arnault tells recruits that the group is “not a faceless company with a distant board” but a family one, where you advance through merit. Both things can be true at once. __A company can be a dream on a CV and still be a hard place to disagree with the boss.__
Copy the attention to detail. Think twice before copying the fear.

Arnault has spent most of his life refusing to explain himself. “Why give out information?” he joked in 2026, when a podcast host complained how little is known about him. But across a Harvard interview in 2001, a long podcast in 2026 and a WWD interview that October, the same few ideas keep coming back. Here are seven of them, each with the story behind it.
1. Make the product. Don't ask the customer.

Arnault once gave a talk to the young marketing team at Louis Vuitton, and he says the boss of the brand was rather embarrassed afterwards. His message to a room full of marketers was that they should not do marketing. Market studies are for supermarket goods, he told them. At this level, the customer follows the product, and you almost have to teach them how to use it.
You must not do marketing. You must create, and it's your products that must impose themselves.
blocks.who: Bernard Arnault, Legend podcast, 2026, as translated by Business Insider

blocks.text: He has been saying this for 25 years. In 2001 he told Harvard Business Review about J'adore, the Dior perfume launched in 1999. People in focus groups said it was fine, just that. It then became, by LVMH's own estimate, one of the top three sellers in the world. Kenzo's Flower did the same. Testers did not know what to make of the bottle or of a poppy, a flower with no scent, yet the Kenzo fragrance group's sales rose 75% in six months.
That's why you should listen to focus groups with only one ear.
Careful. This works for hit products, not for every start-up. Test your assumptions.
2. Total freedom in the studio. Total discipline in the factory.

Two years before that HBR interview, John Galliano sent models down the Dior couture runway in dresses made of newspaper. Most bosses would have stopped him. Arnault did not flinch, and the audience gasped. Dior never planned to sell the paper version. It remade the idea in printed fabric, and that sold well.

Then walk from the studio to the workshop. There, he says, every motion is planned, and a single purse can involve up to ==1,000 manufacturing tasks==. He compared it to the most modern car plants. __The creative part may be chaos, but the part that makes the money is engineering.__ This is the Polytechnique graduate showing up. He says his schooling taught him rigour and how to simplify a hard problem, and he credits his maths professor Laurent Schwartz for showing how clearly a hard subject can be explained.
I don't have alarm bells when it comes to creativity.
3. Think in ten years, not ten weeks.

“What I have in mind every morning is that the desirability of a brand should be as strong in ten years,” he told Forbes in 2019. When luxury spending was slowing in 2024, he told Bloomberg that what he had in mind was 2030. In April 2026, with the shares down about a quarter that year, he told shareholders that what counts is where the group will be in five years.

For example: in 1992 he flew to China for the opening of a Louis Vuitton shop in the basement of a Beijing hotel. There were no cars, he recalled, and not even hot water in the hotel. People on the street all wore the same Mao suits. He rang Vuitton's chief and asked if they were sure they would sell anything. The answer was a firm yes. By 2024 China was LVMH's second-biggest country by sales.

Long-term thinking also means seeing what friends cannot. When he took control of LVMH, an investor friend told him Louis Vuitton was already at its peak, because you saw the bags everywhere. Arnault's answer was that his friend only saw the bags in smart Paris circles. Vuitton was not yet in China, had very limited distribution in the US, and the whole world market was opening up.
“Everyone already has one” usually means everyone you know has one.
4. Stay permanently dissatisfied.

You have already seen this in his meetings. He describes it as a duty. “You must also remain permanently dissatisfied, question yourself constantly, seek out and listen to contradictory views rather than assume you are always right,” he told WWD at 77. He gives the same warning about bosses who think they are always right. Being at the top, he says, is exactly when you need people to argue with you.

It runs in the family. When his grandfather died in June 1959, he put his good school marks into the coffin, because the old man had always watched them so closely. He was ten. His grandmother, franceinfo reports, kept repeating: “Le prix d'excellence, ou rien !” First prize, or nothing. It is not a relaxing way to grow up, and it is hard to separate his success from it.
5. Treat a giant as if it were a start-up.

LVMH has about 220,000 employees and he still tells new recruits to think of it as a start-up. He means it mainly as a war on paperwork. Bureaucracy, papers, reports and regulations slow you down, he says, and you cannot go fast if you are buried in documents that usually serve no purpose.
The idea matters, but anyone can have an idea; what matters most is the execution of that idea.

He gave a nice example to young founders in the same year. When Facebook started, he said, dozens of others were doing almost the same thing with student directories. Only one team made it work. __The idea got dozens of people started. Execution picked the winner.__
Very important for first-time founders! Ideas are cheap. Doing it well isn't.
6. If it isn't fun, you won't last.

At 77, with a fortune counted in the hundreds of billions at its peak, why keep going? His answer is always the same. “Every morning I have fun when I arrive,” he told Bloomberg. In 2026 he said the same in French, adding that working while having fun “permet de travailler beaucoup sans souffrir”: it lets you work a lot without suffering.

It is also why he says he would never go into politics. He lacks the patience and the vocation, he says, and politics means compromises in every direction. He prefers what he does, because it is “très amusant”. When he names the first rule for anyone starting a company, it is the same point: be passionate about the field, and want to work in it.
7. Expect the banker's call. Then hold on.

In 1959 his grandfather died, and the banks began to ask whether they should keep lending to the family firm. His father cancelled the family's seaside holiday that summer and stayed behind. Arnault was ten, and he says it stuck with him, even though it never happened to him later. Decades on, this is the advice he gives founders.
Il faut pas se décourager. La première difficulté, la première fois où le banquier vous appelle en vous disant : ouh là là, attention, le crédit est trop important. Il faut, il faut résister.
blocks.who: Bernard Arnault, Legend podcast, 2026. In English: don't get discouraged the first time the banker rings to say your credit is too high. You have to hold on.

blocks.text: Asked to name the one quality you need to last in business, he laughed: “Je crois qu'il faut être persévérant.” Be persistent. He pairs it with patience, which he told shareholders is always needed in business, and with some honesty about luck. His early adviser Antoine Bernheim used to say the secret was being in the right place at the right time.

For example: his team once wrote off a stake in a US tech fund as lost. When the fund was wound up, it simply posted its shares back to investors, and he received a good pile of a little-known company called Google. It paid off handsomely. It was, he laughed, “une bonne affaire dans laquelle on n'est absolument pour rien”: a good deal we had absolutely nothing to do with.
Rare, this. A billionaire admitting that one of his wins was pure luck.

chapters.title: Chopin, Tennis and a Second-Class Ticket

blocks.text: A lift home in Paris

In October 1990 the pianist Hélène Mercier did not want to go out. The violinist Ivry Gitlis came to fetch her around midnight and took her to the end of a dinner party in Paris. Half an hour after she arrived, a guest offered her a lift home. On the drive, which she remembers as lasting ten or twelve minutes, they talked about the piano, and what he played.

She was Québécoise, trained in Vienna and at Juilliard, and she distrusted businessmen. He invited her to a concert, she says, along with his mother, which she found touching and a little odd. Weeks later, over tea, he sat down and played Chopin's “Revolutionary” Étude, then a piece by Scriabin. The next day she could not get his playing out of her head. They married on ==23 September 1991==.

She had one more surprise. When she was first invited to Dior, his assistant kept saying that Mr Arnault had changed this and had changed that, so she assumed he worked in interior design. It took her a while to understand. When she told him she mistrusted people in business, he defended his work with a line she still quotes: “On ne vend pas des locomotives !” We don't sell locomotives.
Worth noticing. The Terminator won his wife by playing Chopin.

This is his second marriage. He was married to Anne Dewavrin from 1973 to 1990, and they had Delphine and Antoine. With Hélène he had Alexandre, Frédéric and Jean. She rejects the idea of two camps: “Il n'y a qu'une seule famille Arnault,” she told Gala. She says of him that he is more at ease one to one, is “pas un homme de mots”, not a man of words, and that he makes her laugh.
How he raised five heirs

He has thought hard about one fear: rich people's children who buy big cars and spend their nights at parties. He says he has seen it around him. So he showed his children very early how a company worked, talked to them about how he ran his, and told them plainly that without a good education they could not join in.

For example: when one of his sons was preparing for his final school exams, Arnault came home at 6 p.m. to do maths problems with him. The boy was excellent at literature but weak at maths, and he says the shock got him working. Another son was so strong that the father could barely follow. He once sat at the back of a room to hear that son's oral exam for a top school. For thirty minutes the boy stood frozen. Then he filled the board, and scored about 18 out of 20.

His wife was more worried. When the boys were in the gruelling preparatory classes, she feared they had too little freedom and social life. “Leur père ne leur a pas laissé le choix,” she told Gala: their father left them no choice. She encouraged them to find their own identity, and says she did not have children for LVMH. “I am not drawn to heirs or the life of the court,” she told Vogue.
Je pense que, je sais pas si c'est un cadeau, mais [...] c'est le goût du travail.
blocks.who: Bernard Arnault, asked for the best gift he gave his children, Legend podcast, 2026. In English: I don't know if it's a gift, but it is the taste for work.

blocks.text: With grandchildren he is softer. They come to the house regularly and call him “daddy”, and he says they like Coca-Cola and ice cream. “Les petits-enfants, on les voit pour le plaisir,” he says. You raise your children closely. Grandchildren are for pleasure.
The sister he thinks about every day

He rarely talks about grief. In 2026 he talked about his younger sister Dominique, who died of cancer in 2006. They grew up together. She had worked as an auctioneer in the north of France, and when he took over the jeweller Fred, he asked her to run it, which she did successfully. He called her death a catastrophe, and says he thinks of her almost every day.

What he drew from it is practical. She could have caught the illness much earlier, he says, but she told people she had other things to do and felt fine. He now has a check-up every six months, partly because he plays such intense tennis. He does not smoke. He kept the rest short: “Ça fait réfléchir sur la fragilité de l'être humain.” It makes you think about how fragile we are.
Delegate anything you like. Never delegate your own health check.
What he does for pleasure

Music comes first. His father practised the Sibelius violin concerto on Sunday mornings, and that made him want to learn. He won a competition at 13 or 14. In 2017, at 68, he went on stage in Moscow with his wife and his son Frédéric to play Mozart's concerto for three pianos. Paris Match reported that he spent four days rehearsing and struggling to slow his tempo. The audience of 2,000 gave them an ovation.

For example: one day the great pianist Maurizio Pollini came to try out the concert hall at the Fondation Louis Vuitton. He would not play. Hélène refused to play in front of him. So did Frédéric. Then Pollini turned to Arnault: you play a bit, go on. So the head of LVMH climbed on stage and played the first part of Chopin's Second Sonata in front of one of the great pianists of his time. He says he only stopped there because the next movement is really hard.

Tennis is next. Roger Federer is a friend, and they sometimes go on holiday together. Arnault says that when they play doubles on the same side they rarely lose. He is honest about why, comparing himself with Federer the way you might compare his piano playing with Horowitz's. Sport was also part of raising the boys: he still plays with his sons.

Art is the third. In the early 1980s in New York he could not afford Warhol, so he looked for someone cheaper in the galleries, found Jean-Michel Basquiat and bought a few. He says he still has them, and has never sold a painting. Henry Kissinger, he says, was the person who impressed him most, and came to dinner whenever he was in Paris.
He bought Basquiat because he couldn't afford Warhol. Limits can sharpen your eye.
How he spends money

He does live like a billionaire. Specialist press links him to Symphony, a yacht of about 101 metres built by a shipyard that LVMH owns. His polished look is also business: Forbes found him dressed head to toe in his own brands, with a Dior shirt and his initials embroidered on it. But he has some carefully guarded limits, and he enjoys telling people about them.

The private jet is the best story. In 2022, Twitter accounts were tracking every flight by French billionaires and pointing out the pollution. LVMH quietly sold its plane. “The result now is that no one can see where I go because I rent planes when I use private planes,” he said on the radio. __He solved the public problem and kept the private benefit, which is very much his style.__ His son Antoine called the plane a work tool, and said rivals should not be able to see where the family was.

His defence came in 2026. A week's trip through three or four Chinese cities, Macau, Seoul, Japan and Los Angeles is impossible on regular airlines, he said. He also says he takes trains, and once sat in second class to Brussels because the train was full. He recalls his son spotting the head of Mediapart on board, whose site, the son said, kept attacking his flights. “Bon... il n'y a pas eu d'article,” he said. No article appeared.
Giving, and the argument about giving

blocks.text: In March 2020, as hospitals feared running out of supplies, he had Dior, Guerlain and Givenchy perfume factories switch to making hand sanitiser, delivered free to French hospitals. His bigger gifts draw more fire. When Notre-Dame burned, he followed the Pinault family's €100 million pledge with €200 million a few hours later, and the New York Times reported that the spectacle of billionaires trying to top each other fed anger over inequality during the Yellow Vest protests.

He said his family holding company and LVMH would take no tax break on that gift, and hit back at critics: “There's some pettiness and jealousy in the air.” He told the 2026 podcast he had given the Restos money when they were close to collapse, and was attacked for not giving enough. At Notre-Dame's reopening, the host noted, he sat in the tenth row. “Moi, je préfère rester discret,” he said. I prefer to stay discreet.

The Fondation Louis Vuitton is the hardest case. The Frank Gehry building gets about 1.5 million visitors a year, and passes to the city of Paris in time. But France's national audit court found it cost ==€790 million==, against a €100 million figure in the 2006 agreement. It also found group companies cut their tax by ==€518 million== over 11 years. The court did not question the foundation's legality, but said the real return was the image it gave the group. Arnault's reply: the law was voted by Parliament in 2003. “I gave, and this appears suspect.”
Give big and you will still be criticised. Decide why you're giving first.

chapters.title: The Man Who Never Says Luxury

blocks.text: Here is a strange thing about the world's biggest luxury boss. He does not like the word. “Luxury is not a word I am fond of particularly,” he said in 2026, because it suggests frivolity, superficiality and “all that flashy bling”. He wants people to say “high-quality products”, made by artisans. He admits he has lost that battle, since the whole industry and every analyst use the word anyway.

That is his image in small. Every word, suit and shop window is managed, including the ones that look effortless. WWD says that in Paris circles he is known simply as “B.A.”. Forbes called his appearance “a suit of armor”. The press gave him harsher names, including “the Terminator” and “the wolf in cashmere”, and he has outlived them both.
Pick your own words. If you don't, others will pick them for you.
Silence as a strategy

For decades he has mostly spoken at LVMH's annual meetings and results days. La revue des médias traces his retreat from long interviews to one bad experience. In 2014 he opened his doors and appeared on camera for France 2's Complément d'enquête. LVMH then filed a complaint alleging blackmail against a journalist working on the programme, who denied wrongdoing, and the investigation ended with the case dismissed. After that his appearances shrank.

So when he did talk, in 2026, it was a calculated choice. The host of Legend, which bills itself as France's top podcast, spent a year and a half getting the interview, first through a WhatsApp call to the group's head of external relations, then by meeting Antoine, then Bernard. Arnault picked a long, friendly format that its host says has never claimed to be journalism. __He skipped the journalists and went straight to the audience, and a young one at that.__
Ça me laisse complètement froid. Et dans la plupart des cas, je ne regarde même pas.
blocks.who: Bernard Arnault on press coverage of him, Legend podcast, 2026, as printed by BFM. In English: it leaves me completely cold, and in most cases I don't even look.

blocks.text: You should read that with care. Less than three weeks later he published a three-page reply to Le Monde. And a June 2026 article in La revue des médias says he reads and sees everything. The man who says he does not care has spent 40 years caring very much. Saying you don't care is part of the armour.
Notice the gap between what he says and what he does here.
The product as the headline

His best publicity stunts look like small favours. He tells this one himself. In 1995, Madame Chirac rang him two or three days before Princess Diana came to Paris to open a Cézanne show, asking for a gift idea. Dior was working on a new quilted leather bag. He and Sidney Toledano spent half a day on it. Madame Chirac gave it to Diana, who loved it and carried it around the world. It became the Lady Dior.

And at his company's 2026 annual meeting he wore a Louis Vuitton watch with a tiny moving Einstein on the dial, whose eye winks and whose tongue pokes out. Only two were made, he says. He quoted Einstein to the shareholders while wearing it. Even his wrist was doing a job.

blocks.text: The Musk lunch shows how he stages things. The hotel's three-Michelin-star chef had already left for the summer season in Saint-Tropez. He came back to Paris at Arnault's request to cook it. Maye Musk came too, and Antoine put the photos on Instagram. It said everything without a word: the two richest people on Earth, on LVMH's terrace, eating LVMH's food.
The day he joined X

For 77 years he had no social media account of his own. Then Le Monde ran a six-part series in July 2026 on his power, media holdings, tax and family, ending with a piece on rivalry among his children. Le Monde's main shareholder is Xavier Niel, the partner of his daughter Delphine, which made the whole thing very awkward at Paris dinner tables.

His reply, titled “Merci”, went out on 26 July on LVMH's press account. It was funny, and it had a blade in it. He thanked the paper for its “heavy artillery” and apologised to readers for the group's “failure of bodily diversity”, after the series commented on how slim everyone is. He pleaded “guilty” to having talked to five French presidents. The next day he opened @BernardArnault to share it. Elon Musk reposted him.
My children run Houses, build teams, make decisions, and—sacrilege—call each other on Sundays. What, in an ordinary family, is called a Sunday is called, in ours, an intrigue.
blocks.who: Bernard Arnault, open letter to Le Monde, July 2026, as quoted by Fortune

blocks.text: Fortune counted 4.5 million views in 24 hours. It was a real lesson in tone, because irony made him look relaxed. It also had limits. WWD noted he never mentioned the speculation over who will succeed him. And he added a remark that says a lot about how he works: he argued that Le Monde had been harsher on him than on the Wertheimer family of Chanel, who declined to take part. “Let that serve as a lesson for your next subjects.”
Owning the press

He is not only a subject of news. LVMH's media arm includes the business daily Les Echos, the popular paper Le Parisien, Investir, Radio Classique and stakes in L'Opinion and Challenges, and he co-founded the VivaTech tech fair. He told a Senate inquiry in 2022 that the media unit was marginal for the group, with €400 million in sales and losses. He has also called owning it a form of philanthropy.
Si demain « les Echos » défendaient l'économie marxiste, je serais extrêmement gêné.

blocks.text: LVMH is also among the biggest advertisers in the French print press. That gives him a second lever, and we cover how he has used it in the next chapter. It is one reason his critics say he has too much power, and he points to the Le Monde series itself as proof that he cannot silence anyone.
How different countries see him

In **France** he is admired and resented in the same breath. He is the country's richest person, its great exporter, and a constant target. “En France, quand on réussit un peu, immédiatement on est critiqué,” he says. In France, succeed a little and you are criticised at once. In 2025, 86% of those polled backed the wealth tax he attacked. He also says the group has paid €40 billion to the French state over the years, and he makes the case often.

In **America** the mood is warmer, and he likes it. Trump praised him in Texas in 2019 as “a visionary” and “an artist, really”. Arnault says he has known Trump since his New York days in the 1980s and calls him a friend. In September 2024 he and Alexandre went to dinner at Trump's Florida home on the very day of the second assassination attempt. Trump, he says, greeted their sympathy with “Two to zero.”
Same man, two countries. Home is rarely your easiest audience.

In **China**, what matters most is the customers. He first visited in 1992 and got in early. LVMH has since built its fortune partly on Chinese shoppers, which is why the slowdown there hurts so much. The numbers are in the last chapter.
And in India

Indian readers mostly know him through two stories: a rich list, and a rent bill. In 2023 lease papers from Reliance's Jio World Plaza in Mumbai showed Louis Vuitton paying about ==₹40.5 lakh a month== for 7,365 square feet, its biggest store in India. Indian media loved the framing of one billionaire paying rent to another. One headline in 2025 simply read: “This man pays Rs 40 lakh to Mukesh Ambani per month”.

blocks.text: The big moment was Dior's show at the Gateway of India on 30 March 2023, the first time a fashion house had unveiled a new line in the country. Models walked over marigolds. Isha Ambani and Radhika Merchant were among the guests, and Mumbai's Chanakya ateliers were put in the spotlight. Bloomberg pointed out the deeper shift: Indian hands had worked for European luxury for years, largely out of view.

India also came up in one of his sharpest complaints about France. In 2013, angry at his treatment at home, he told Le Monde: “Mr Tata is a star in India, like Warren Buffett in the United States.” His point was that those countries celebrate their entrepreneurs, while “in France we condemn wealth”. For a young Indian founder it is worth seeing yourself through his eyes. __From Paris, India looked like a place that loves its builders.__
Remember this line the next time someone tells you India hates ambition.

It is easy to admire the empire and skip this part. Don't. Many of the things Arnault got wrong came from the same qualities that made him rich: speed, secrecy, and a refusal to be told no. We have tried to be exact about what was proved, what was settled and what was only alleged. He was never charged in the spying case, and the settlements below did not admit guilt.
The promise he broke

When he took over the bankrupt Boussac group in 1984, the French state was closely involved, and he made commitments on jobs. In 2026 he said it plainly himself: there were about 12,000 people, “on s'était engagé à en garder dix mille et on n'a pas tenu cet engagement”. We promised to keep 10,000, and we did not keep that promise. He blames worse-than-expected factories and Chinese competition. The French press called him the Terminator.

His defence is scale: the group now employs about 220,000 people directly, and he says it supports about 200,000 jobs in France once suppliers are counted. He also says the state's loan was repaid with extra, and that the group has paid about €40 billion in tax and social charges since. “On peut peut-être arrêter un jour de ressortir ça,” he said. Maybe one day we can stop bringing that up. Forty years on, people have not.
A broken promise can outlive the company you broke it for. Promise less.
The stake he kept hidden

You have read the Hermès story in an earlier chapter. Here is the verdict. France's market regulator found in June 2013 that LVMH had concealed each stage of its stake-building. It used equity swaps through foreign subsidiaries, split among three banks. It fined the company ==€8 million==, then its largest ever fine. LVMH called the decision “totally unjustified”, said it would appeal, and then dropped the appeal.

The regulator admitted that those swaps did not break disclosure rules on their own. What it punished was the overall scheme and the delay in telling the market. Under a 2014 peace deal, LVMH handed its Hermès shares to its own shareholders. So he made a large gain, and he still did not get Hermès. __The family he tried to out-manoeuvre came out with stronger defences, and he came out with a reputation.__
Legal step by step isn't the same as safe. Regulators judge the whole picture.
The passport that blew up in his face

In September 2012, with France debating a 75% tax on top incomes, news broke that he had applied for Belgian citizenship. Libération ran him on the front page under the words “Casse-toi riche con !”, roughly “Get lost, rich idiot”. He sued. LVMH brands pulled advertising from the paper, which cost it about €150,000, and other luxury brands followed in solidarity, for a reported total of up to €700,000. That issue's sales rose 27%.

His explanation was about family, not tax. He said he wanted to protect a Belgian foundation holding the empire in case his heirs fell out after his death, and he said he would stay a French taxpayer. Critics pointed to Belgium's far lower inheritance tax. Belgian prosecutors and the immigration office gave negative opinions. In April 2013 he gave up: “J'ai sous-estimé l'impact de cette démarche.” I underestimated the impact.

It took four more years to end. In June 2017 a Brussels court confirmed that its inquiry into whether he had falsely claimed Belgian residence was closed, after he paid an undisclosed sum without admitting guilt. WWD's source put it at tens of thousands of euros. He also ultimately resumed normal relations with Libération. The cost in money was trivial. The cost in image lasted more than a decade.
He was told it would stay secret. Assume nothing stays secret.
The spy on the payroll

In 2013 a former head of French domestic intelligence, Bernard Squarcini, began working as a consultant for LVMH. One job involved François Ruffin, a journalist whose satirical film Merci Patron! mocked Arnault through a couple who lost their jobs when a Kenzo suit factory moved to Poland. A Paris court later found Squarcini complicit in the illegal surveillance of Ruffin and his paper Fakir, as they planned to disrupt an LVMH shareholder meeting.

In December 2021 a Paris judge approved a deal in which LVMH paid ==€10 million== to close the probe into its role. It was not an admission of guilt, and LVMH's legal chief told the court there was no institutional system of spying, though the group accepted its responsibilities. Ruffin said justice could be bought cheaply, and his appeals failed. In November 2025 a judge cleared the way for his separate civil case over invasion of privacy.

Arnault took the stand as a witness in November 2024. “I was completely unaware,” he said, and “I am here as a witness, a simple witness.” He told the court the surveillance was ordered by a close associate who has since died, and that he never knew. In March 2025 Squarcini was found guilty and given four years, two suspended, and a €200,000 fine. His lawyers said he would appeal. Ruffin's lawyer regretted Arnault's absence from the defendants. Arnault has not been accused of a crime in the trial.

His own comment on the film in 2026 was that it was “assez rigolo”, pretty funny, and “bourré d'erreurs”, full of errors. The real lesson does not depend on who is right. Here was a €10 million bill, a public trial and a decade of headlines, all to manage one small left-wing newspaper. __The attempt to control a story became a much bigger story than the film.__
Read this twice. Never spy on critics. Answer them.
The press he leaned on

Spying is the extreme case. There is also a quieter pattern. In March 2016 unions at Le Parisien, which LVMH had just bought, said their editor had banned reviews of Merci Patron!. In November 2017 Le Canard enchaîné reported that LVMH had cancelled ads in Le Monde after its Paradise Papers stories on his offshore holdings, which he said tax authorities knew about. LVMH denied cutting all advertising. In 2024 came the memo banning staff from talking to named outlets.

Everyone who has run a company knows the urge. If you are powerful enough, you can often act on it, and that is exactly why it is dangerous. A reporter quoted by La revue des médias says the Squarcini affair helped create a climate of fear around covering the group. That is not a reputation any founder should want.
The workshops he didn't check

His whole pitch is craftsmanship, which is why this one hurts most. In June 2024 a Milan court put a Dior handbag unit under court administration after a probe alleged it had subcontracted work to Chinese-owned firms that mistreated workers. In July 2025 the same happened to Loro Piana. The court papers described workers putting in up to 90 hours a week for as little as €4 an hour on cashmere jackets, in illegal workshops.

For example: one intermediary told police it made thousands of jackets a year for between €118 and €128 each. The jackets often sell for over €3,000. Loro Piana says those figures don't reflect what it paid or the full cost of materials, and says it dropped the supplier as soon as it learned of the subcontracting in May 2025.

To be fair about the outcomes: courts ended both measures early, Dior's in February 2025 and Loro Piana's in April 2026, after the companies tightened control of their suppliers. Italy's competition authority closed its Dior probe “without establishing any infringement”, with Dior committing €2 million over five years to help victims of labour exploitation. Even so, the Milan court's finding on Loro Piana was that it had failed to adequately control its own supply chain.
If your name is on it, you own the whole chain.
The genius he backed, and lost

In 2001 Harvard Business Review, summing up his view, wrote that you don't “manage” John Galliano. In February 2011 a video showed Galliano in a Paris bar saying “I love Hitler”. Dior suspended him, then fired him days before its show, after 15 years. Dior's chief, Sidney Toledano, called the words odious. Galliano told a court he had addictions and could not recall the insults, and was found guilty, with a suspended €6,000 fine.

Arnault's handling was fast and cold. He stayed silent during the crisis and skipped the show. The very next morning, he announced the Bulgari deal, and the market moved on. Months later he shut the door publicly: “He will not be working for LVMH.” And then the personal note: “he didn't have the simple politeness to contact me.” If you tolerate brilliant people's chaos for 15 years, you are also taking on the risk that one day it explodes.
The investments that went badly, or too well

Part of the empire's record is a list of side bets that lost money, which an earlier chapter covers in detail. His stake in the retailer Carrefour, taken with Colony Capital in 2007, had lost close to €2 billion by 2011, and he only finished selling out in 2021. He does not usually dwell on these. Ask for his regret and he gives you a different one.
I sold my Netflix stake too early; it has since multiplied tenfold!

He says his team held nearly 20% of Netflix at the start. Note what he chooses to confess: a mistake that still made money. He also rejects a failure that everyone else lists, his first American property deal, the Princess building. Google shows it as his great flop, he told the podcast, and he says it was among his most profitable deals ever. We could not settle that, so read it as his version.
The fights he picks in public

In September 2025 he went after the economist Gabriel Zucman, who had proposed a 2% yearly tax on fortunes over €100 million. Arnault called him “first and foremost a far-left activist” with “a pseudo-academic competence”, and said the plan was “a clearly stated desire to destroy the French economy”. Zucman, a professor, replied that he had never belonged to any party or movement, and that such language was close to that of Trump and Musk.

He has a real argument about taxing business assets, and many in French business agreed. But polls showed 86% of the French public in favour of the tax, and a personal attack handed the economist a bigger platform. Earlier that year he had said that coming home from Washington to French tax plans was “a bit of a cold shower”. Cash Investigation later showed how little personal tax a controlling shareholder can pay when dividends stay in a holding company, which is legal. France's public-TV ethics committee felt the show could have offered more balance.
The question he refuses to answer

The biggest risk is still open. Back in 2013 he said he preferred relative fragility and trusted his family to stay united. In 2026 investors told Reuters that the lack of clarity about who comes next was becoming a risk, and one shareholder called the plan “uncertain and opaque”. His answer in April: ask again in seven or eight years. We cannot say he is wrong, because the test has not come yet. But every founder should know that leaving this question open may suit you, and not necessarily the company after you.

blocks.text: Add up the fines and they are tiny next to €80 billion of annual sales. That is the trap. He could absorb every one of these costs, and most young founders could not. __If you copy his aggression without his balance sheet, one such mistake will end you.__ Copy the detail, the patience and the love of the product. Leave the swaps, the spy and the blacklist behind.

On 23 April 2026 Arnault walked on stage at the Carrousel du Louvre for LVMH's annual meeting, wearing his winking Einstein watch. The shares were down about a quarter that year. For the first time, all five of his children spoke to the shareholders. A 25-year-old investor stood up, and Arnault congratulated him on buying the shares. “It's a good time. I do it too, each at our own scale.”

Then someone asked the obvious question: who comes next? He pointed to the 99% vote the year before, which lets him stay in his roles until he is 85. “So we'll talk about all that again in seven or eight years,” he said. Looking at his children, he added: do they seem very ambitious? Warren Buffett, Bloomberg reported in 2024, once wrote to tell him he was wrong to set the age limit at 80, because it was too low.
He'd be 85 in 2034. He means it.

blocks.text: Those numbers show how far he has fallen, on paper. In December 2022 he was the richest person alive. On 10 September 2026 he dropped out of Bloomberg's top ten, reportedly for the first time since 2017. Bloomberg's index shows his wealth down about ==$61.5 billion== in a year. The shares traded at their lowest since late 2020 after October's sales figures. None of this money has been spent. It is simply the value of his LVMH stake, marked down daily.

He is also still chairman and CEO, not a figurehead. Early in 2026 the family crossed 50% of LVMH's capital, partly because he keeps buying, and he says so openly. “When the shares drop a little, as has been the case for some time, I buy more,” he told shareholders. Reports put his purchases in 2025 at about €1.4 billion, at an average price far above where the stock now trades. __Whatever else you think of him, he is backing his view with his own money.__
You just need to be patient. In business, in fact, you always have to be patient.
blocks.who: Bernard Arnault, to shareholders, April 2026, as reported by Vogue

blocks.text: The business he has now

LVMH's 2025 revenue was €80.8 billion, down from €84.7 billion in 2024, with profit from recurring operations of €17.8 billion. For the first nine months of 2026, sales reached €57.1 billion, up 2% on an organic basis. The picture inside is mixed: fashion and leather goods fell 5% in the third quarter on weak Chinese demand, while jewellery and Sephora did well. L'Oréal has passed LVMH as France's largest company by market value.

His response follows the old playbook. He sold Marc Jacobs, which closed on 1 September 2026, and sold more of the DFS duty-free assets. He gave Dior to a new designer, Jonathan Anderson, and credited Anderson's first designs for the growth in the second quarter. He talks of paying “very close attention to margins”, while still spending on the things that make people want the brands, such as the new Louis Vuitton stores in Beijing and Seoul.
Sell the side bets. Back the stars. Same move he made in 2002.
His current bets

**Tiffany.** He bought it for nearly $16 billion, and he wants it to be “the world's leading jewellery brand” within five years. “We are not far off, but we are not there yet,” he said in April. **Formula 1.** LVMH signed a ten-year partnership and says it is the sport's first partner. Before the Monaco Grand Prix, Max Verstappen took him round the streets at ==250 km/h==. “Well, Verstappen was driving, so I told myself the risk is limited.”

**AI.** At VivaTech in June 2026 he said he takes part in weekly design sessions using generative AI to develop product ideas. Louis Vuitton designers use it to test colours and materials, and Sephora launched an app inside ChatGPT. **Football.** His children pushed him to buy control of Paris FC in 2024, with Red Bull as a partner. He told them they had to reach the top division, which they did. Next he wants a place in European competition, without it costing too much. The club lost €33.5 million in 2025.

**Control.** In September 2026 the family proposed folding its holding companies together, so that Christian Dior would become a limited partnership renamed Agache, holding almost all of the family's LVMH stake. Michelin and Hermès use similar structures, which make hostile bids much harder. He would remain its manager, alongside Agache Commandité, the vehicle set up for his children, who hold 20% each. Filings say decisions there need three of the five. It is the Hermès defence, built by the man who once ran into it.
He lost to Hermès's structure. Now his family uses the same legal form.
The succession question

All five children hold senior jobs: Delphine runs Christian Dior Couture, Antoine runs Christian Dior SE and LVMH's image, Alexandre is deputy CEO of Moët Hennessy, Frédéric runs Loro Piana, and Jean runs Louis Vuitton watches. Four sit on the board. He has named no one. Morningstar's analyst sees Delphine as closest to the top, and thinks a professional outsider is also possible. The best-performing division this year, jewellery and watches, is run by none of them, as Fortune pointed out.
On progresse chez LVMH par un système de méritocratie.

blocks.text: He adds another line: “Ils sont tous encore jeunes, donc tout va bien.” They are all still young, so all is well. The eldest is 51. He says the question is about results, and he clearly does not feel he has to decide. Investors and journalists keep asking. Their worry is that one day the decision will not be his to make, and a family that promises it will never split will be tested.

In July he said his foundation would show, from October, a Van Gogh self-portrait with the bandaged ear that he calls the equal of the Mona Lisa, and that its owner is a friend. His critics call him an oligarch. WWD calls him one of the chief architects of modern luxury. He would say he is only getting started.
Un leader mondial français [...] qui a encore beaucoup de potentiel et qui n'en est qu'au début. Et donc j'ai encore beaucoup d'années pour m'amuser à gérer LVMH [...]

blocks.text: Asked how he wants to be remembered, he laughed first: as late as possible, please. Then he named the thing he is proudest of: starting from a struggling firm in Roubaix and creating France's largest listed company and a world leader in its field. It is no longer the largest, as it happens. If you are reading this at 17, you will find out alongside everyone else how the last act goes. So far, he intends to write it himself.
Seventy-seven. Down tens of billions. Still in the shops on Saturday.

lessons.title: Go and see for yourself.
lessons.text: Arnault still walks through his stores on Saturday mornings at 77, and sends notes about chairs and salespeople's shoes. He learned it at five or six, on building sites with his grandfather. You will not find these things in a spreadsheet, so go to where your customer actually is.

lessons.title: Never get comfortable with good news.
lessons.text: Bloomberg reported that the worst way to start a meeting with him is to say that sales are robust. He calls it staying permanently dissatisfied. Celebrate for an hour, then ask what could be better.

lessons.title: Love the product more than the pitch.
lessons.text: He told Louis Vuitton's own marketing team not to do marketing, and J'adore became a global hit after focus groups called it merely fine. Listen to your testers with one ear, as he says. But remember he could afford the misses, so keep your bets small while you are young.

lessons.title: Give talent freedom, and give the process rules.
lessons.text: Galliano could make dresses out of newspaper, while a single purse could have 1,000 planned steps in the workshop. Be loose where ideas are born and strict where money is made. Most young companies do this exactly backwards.

lessons.title: Think in ten-year chunks.
lessons.text: In 1992 he visited a China with no cars on the street and no hot water in his hotel, and Vuitton opened a store there anyway. It later became LVMH's second-biggest country. Ask where your market will be in 2036, not next quarter.

lessons.title: Expect the banker's call, and hold on.
lessons.text: When his grandfather died in 1959, the banks got nervous and his father cancelled the family holiday to stay and defend the firm. Arnault's advice to founders today is not to panic at the first scary call. Persistence, he says, is the one quality you need.

lessons.title: Execute. Ideas are cheap.
lessons.text: He reminds founders that dozens of teams had something like Facebook, and only one made it work. He tries to run a giant like a start-up by fighting paperwork. Spend your energy on doing the thing, not on protecting your idea.

lessons.title: Choose people, then keep them.
lessons.text: Michael Burke came as an intern and was still with him more than four decades later. Sidney Toledano got a call at 9 a.m. on his first day, and stayed for 30 years. Loyalty compounds like money, and lying is the one thing Arnault says he won't forgive.

lessons.title: Be careful what you promise.
lessons.text: He promised to keep 10,000 Boussac jobs, by his own account, and admits he did not. Forty years later people still bring it up, and he is still answering. Promise only what you can deliver, even when a promise would help you win the deal.

lessons.title: Secrets get out, so plan for it.
lessons.text: He was told his Belgian citizenship request would stay discreet, and it ended up on a front page as “Get lost, rich idiot”. He says he underestimated the impact, and it took him years to shake off. Before any clever move, ask how it would look as a headline.

lessons.title: Answer your critics. Don't watch them.
lessons.text: A film mocked him, and his company ended up paying €10 million to close a spying probe, while a consultant was convicted and has appealed. In 2026 he answered Le Monde with a funny letter that drew 4.5 million views in a day. One approach cost years of bad press. The other cost three pages.

lessons.title: Check your whole supply chain.
lessons.text: Italian courts put the makers of Dior bags and Loro Piana jackets under supervision for failing to police their suppliers, and released both early once they fixed their controls. If you sell quality, you own every step, including the ones you outsource. Visit your suppliers before a prosecutor does.

lessons.title: Control what matters.
lessons.text: He beat rivals by buying stakes they didn't see coming, then lost to the Hermès family because they had locked up voting control. Today his family holds 50% of LVMH's capital and about two-thirds of the votes. Know exactly who owns what in your company, and understand it before you need it.

lessons.title: Do something you'd do for free.
lessons.text: “Every morning I have fun when I arrive,” he says, and he stops for 20-minute piano breaks at work. Enjoying it is how he works so hard without suffering, he says. If you dread Monday at 25, you will not last until 77.

lessons.title: Decide who comes after you, or decide that you won't.
lessons.text: He has spent years building structures to keep the empire together, yet still says “seven or eight years” when asked who is next. Investors call that a growing risk. Even if you are 20, build something that doesn't need you to be there, because that is what makes it worth owning.

factCheck.method: Each factual sentence is tied to the sources listed. Arnault's own words come mainly from the full French transcript of the July 2026 Legend podcast, read directly, plus WWD (Oct 2026) and Harvard Business Review (2001). Where a quote appears in French, it is verbatim from the source and the English under it is our translation; quotes in English are verbatim as printed by the named outlet. Bloomberg's 2024 feature blocked automated reading, so details and quotes from it were taken from search excerpts and from a Founders podcast transcript in which the host reads the article aloud. Those lines should be compared with the Bloomberg original at final check. The WSJ, Reuters and Forbes 2019 pieces were read through search excerpts and corroborating coverage, not full text. A Wall Street Journal Magazine archive copy was not read, because access to it was refused, and we did not use it.

disputed.note: Forbes 2019 has him starting at home at 6:30 and in the office by about 8. Bloomberg 2024 says 8 a.m. to 8:30 p.m. franceinfo 2026 says at his desk by 8:30. We give each attributed.

disputed.claim: How many stores he visits in a day
disputed.note: Fortune says as many as 25 in a day, and in one version says 25 'of his own stores'; another Fortune line includes competitors. Bloomberg's opening describes 'a few hours' on Saturday mornings. The 25 is a maximum, not routine.

In 2026 Arnault said there were about 12,000 staff and a pledge to keep 10,000. INA's 1984 archive, as cited in part 2 of this book, describes going from 15,000 to 12,000; reports of total cuts reach about 9,000. Arnault's figure of 'two thousand' jobs is therefore his own framing. Part 2's disputed list has the other numbers.

In the Legend podcast he says his family group put in 50 million francs, with investors bringing the total to 400 million, plus a repayable state loan of about the same size. Part 2 uses 90 million from his side, from Les Echos 1996 and a Finance Ministry note. Not stated in this part beyond the loan being repaid, which is his claim and LVMH's. France Télévisions and Audrey Millet describe public aid of 633 to 940 million francs.

Arnault tells it as a rushed gift for Diana at Madame Chirac's request, in 1995. Toledano says he had been developing the bag since 1994. Bloomberg, as read in the Founders transcript, focuses on Diana being photographed with it in Argentina in 1995. The accounts can be reconciled, but Arnault's version has no independent witness in our sources. We attribute it to him. Exact month of the Paris visit not checked.

At the April 2016 AGM he reportedly said he had not seen it. In 2026 he said he had watched it because so many people mentioned it. These may simply be different dates. The 2016 line comes from French Wikipedia's citation and is left out of the text.

Many profiles describe his 1980s Florida/US property venture as a failure, and part 1 discusses his time in America. Arnault says in 2026 it was among his most profitable property deals and that the failure story is simply wrong. He offered Michael Burke as a witness. We could not verify the accounts and present it as his version.

Arnault says he held 'almost 20%' at the start, Business Insider reports that claim, and part 2 dates the bet to 1999. We found no filing confirming 20%, so it is attributed to him. His 'multiplied tenfold' is also his own estimate.

disputed.claim: How long the Legend interview ran
disputed.note: WWD says 1 hour 40 minutes and the transcript shows 100 minutes. BFM says over two hours, and 21 News says nearly three. We avoid stating the length in the text.

Fortune, citing the Financial Times and La Lettre, dates it 17 January 2024. La revue des médias says 19 January, and lists seven outlets including Mediapart and Le Canard enchaîné. We say January 2024 and 'a named list'.

Le Monde, as cited by Puremédias, put LVMH's own withdrawn ads at €150,000 and total losses at up to €700,000 including other brands. La revue des médias attributes the full €700,000 to LVMH. We use the Le Monde split.

disputed.claim: Cost of the Fondation Louis Vuitton
disputed.note: Vogue in 2014 said about $135 million, which was far off. The Telegraph said about $900 million, unconfirmed. The Cour des comptes found €790 million, against €100 million in the 2006 agreement. Some critics allege overbilling, but the court did not establish that, so we do not say it.

Arnault told shareholders no deduction would apply to the family holding or to LVMH, having hit its ceiling. Some critics assumed tax breaks would apply, as the rules allowed 60–90% in general. We found no independent audit of the actual tax treatment, so this is his statement.

disputed.claim: How long Squarcini's sentence would be served
disputed.note: Reports say four years with two suspended. France 24 expected the two-year term to be served with an electronic tag, while La revue des médias describes it as 'deux fermes'. He appealed; we found no appeal ruling as of 3 November 2026. A separate civil case by Ruffin was cleared to go ahead in November 2025, and we found no outcome.

Reuters reports Arnault telling the court that the surveillance was ordered by a close associate who died in 2018. La revue des médias says Arnault was preoccupied by Ruffin and that Squarcini acted for LVMH. Ruffin's side regrets Arnault was not a defendant. Arnault was only a witness, was never charged, and denies knowing. We state this precisely and do not imply otherwise.

AFP pieces in 2026 say LVMH voted the rise to 85 in 2022. Vogue, Fortune and Observer say 2022 raised the CEO limit to 80, and 2025 raised both roles to 85. We follow the latter, and the Buffett letter, from Bloomberg via Founders, refers to the earlier step to 80.

Bloomberg: $132bn, #14 on 1 Nov 2026. Forbes, with family: $117.4bn on 1 Oct 2026 per Sportune (and the profile fragment of this book gives $117.4bn at #17 on 1 Nov 2026). Sportune says #14 on Forbes on 1 Oct; Billionaires.Africa says #17 on 13 Oct. Forbes and Bloomberg differ in method and date.

The Benzinga piece names Frédéric as head of watches and Alexandre as head of wines and spirits; Observer, Vogue and Fortune give Frédéric at Loro Piana and Alexandre as deputy CEO of Moët Hennessy under Jean-Jacques Guiony. Jean's title also varies, from head of LV watches to overseeing the watch division. We follow Vogue and the podcast.

French sources in a secondary site date his election to December 2024, while Le Nouvel Obs dates his entry to January 2026. Election and formal entry are different events, so we give no date in the text.

Vogue: a ride of about ten minutes. Gala: twelve minutes. La Presse, from her 2009 book, gives October 1990 and says they met again three weeks later. Paris Match says he played the Chopin étude 27 years before 2017. Marie Claire adds that they spoke only about piano. These fit, apart from the length of the car ride.

disputed.claim: How many Einstein watches, and the watch he wore
disputed.note: Arnault says two examples of the Louis Vuitton automaton watch were made. Vogue says he wore a Tambour Einstein at the AGM. We assume these are the same model, which neither source states outright. Treat as probable.
Forbes had him briefly top on 7 December 2022; Bloomberg's index moved on 13 December 2022. We cite Bloomberg.
